newsitem.title: USA: Speedy ruling sought in Tampa stadium bond case.
newsitem.headline: Speedy ruling sought in Tampa stadium bond case.

text.p: Florida's Hillsborough County has sought an expedited ruling in the latest litigation over public financing for the Tampa Bay Buccaneers' new $168 football stadium, County Attorney Emeline Acton said Tuesday.

Tampa Sports Authority planned to issue revenue bonds for the stadium via Smith Barney Inc in early November. If the Second District U.S. Court of Appeals agrees to fast-track the case, a ruling on the financing plan could be delivered by Oct 31, Acton said.

However, the plaintiffs' attorneys have said they would object to fast-track status. Because of that, Acton said it was likely the bond issue would proceed but that the bond documents would carry a notice of the pending litigation and a legal opinion that the lawsuit was without merit.
I would recommend they do that because I don't think ultimately we're going to lose this case," Acton said.
Former Tampa Mayor William Poe, who has twice sued the county to block the financing plan, appealed the dismissal of the second lawsuit Monday before Second District U.S. Court of Appeals.
Poe's lawsuit challenged the constitutionality of using public tax money to build a stadium that would primarily benefit the private, for-profit team.
On Sept 3, voters approved a half-cent sales tax increase that will raise $2.7 billion over 30 years for schools, roads, public safety and the stadium.
Before the election, Poe sued unsuccessfully to have the referendum removed from the ballot on grounds that it would unconstitutionally use public money for a private purpose.

He sued a second time after the referendum, saying that in the first case, the judge had been legally barred from considering the stadium issue separately from the other projects to be funded with the sales tax hike.
Circuit Judge Sam Pendino dismissed that lawsuit on Oct 4, ruling that it raised the same issues that had already been litigated. Poe appealed that ruling on Monday.

Even if fast-track status is granted, it would not preclude the possibility of further appeals if Poe loses again. Acton said that unless the county issues the bonds by the end of the year, it could run into new conflicts with U.S. Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan's bill, which would ban tax-exempt funding of professional sports stadiums.
"The Moynihan bill is going to be reintroduced the first week of January. That gives us further concern and further reason to hurry up and market these things," Acton said.
Despite the pending litigation, Acton said she was confident that "they're going to be sold."
